doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

title: Ellington, Phil Spector and Dot Records producers
summary: Hank says he never worked with Ellington or Spector, then praises Dot producer Tom Mack and tells of producers demanding cuts, called flying F cuts.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Before we wrap up here, I wanted to ask you about two individuals. Duke Ellington. Did you work with Ellington?
No, I never worked with Phil Spector thank God.

No, not at all. I mean I worked with some great producers, I mean going back to Dot Records, Tom Mack who did Harry James and a lot of big bands, Woody Herman and I got really tight with some of those producers at Dot and it was really great to do those. I worked with Tom Mack, we worked with somebody in the big bands, he was in Glenn Miller’s original band. He was a producer at Dot Records. And you know he was just great to work with. They were great musicians so it was really great to work with him. Guys like that. The guys that you didn’t want to work with were those guys, the artist would say, “I want to make a cut.” If a guy wanted to make a cut in a certain place and you knew it was wrong and you tried to tell them it was wrong and they don’t want to be embarrassed by the fact that they’re talking to you and they’ve got you in the wrong place. You’ve got to gently, you know I’ve done a couple of times. They’ll say, “Cut it right there” and you know you can’t cut it there because the brass section is playing. You don’t say anything, just move the tape up, you know, make the cut and let it go. Sometimes a producer — we used to call them [deliberately inaudible].
You used to call them what?
“Cut it there.” “Cut it where? Where’s the downbeat, where do you want me to cut it?” And if you cut it in the wrong place, you’re not a mind reader.
